title: How State Insurance Regulators are Responding to Growth in CLOs and Private Credit
date_evidence: PDF title page: "How State Insurance Regulators are Responding to Growth in CLOs and Private Credit / April 2026"
key_claim: The NAIC's own account of its response to insurer private-credit growth. US insurers held $276.8 billion of CLOs at year-end 2024, about 5.1% of total bonds and 3.1% of total cash and invested assets; life insurers held 82% of that exposure and insurers with more than $10 billion in assets accounted for 82% of it; about 80% was rated investment grade or higher and 39% AAA. The brief lists the instruments in play: enhanced private-placement disclosure from 2026 reporting, the principles-based bond definition effective 1 January 2025, a 45% RBC charge on CLO residual tranches, AG 53 and AG 55, and a due diligence framework for credit rating providers plus an adopted discretion process to challenge ratings used for regulatory purposes.
frame_summary: State insurance regulators are arguing that private credit and CLOs are not inherently unsuitable for insurance portfolios, and that the live regulatory question is whether capital treatment, disclosure and supervision keep pace with the structures, which justifies reducing what the NAIC calls blind reliance on third-party credit ratings.
verbatim_quote: has adopted a discretion process to challenge ratings for regulatory use when they do not reasonably reflect investment risk
verbatim_list: NAIC is developing a due diligence framework for credit rating providers and has adopted a discretion process to challenge ratings for regulatory use when they do not reasonably reflect investment risk.
U.S. insurers held $276.8 billion in CLOs at year-end 2024, up about 2 percent from year-end 2023, representing about 5.1 percent of total bonds and 3.1 percent of total cash and invested assets.
Overall credit quality remained relatively strong, with about 80 percent of insurer CLO holdings rated investment grade or higher, including about 39 percent rated AAA.
Life insurers held 82 percent of all insurer CLO investments at year-end 2024, and insurers with more than $10 billion in assets accounted for 82 percent of total exposure.
Regulators have also increased the RBC charge on CLO residual tranches to 45 percent and continue to evaluate capital treatment for other asset-backed security exposures.
Beginning with 2026 reporting, insurers must provide more granular disclosures on private placements and other similar complex investments.

title: Regulatory Update: NAIC Adopts New Risk-Based Capital Charges for Collateral Loans and Collateralized Loan Obligations
key_claim: Two June 2026 adoptions. On 11 June the Life Risk-Based Capital (E) Working Group replaced the uniform 6.8% RBC charge on collateral loans with a look-through framework keyed to the underlying collateral and to overcollateralisation bands, effective for RBC reported as of 31 December 2027. On 23 June the RBC IRE Working Group adopted Proposal 2026-12-IRE, introducing CLO C-1 factors that turn on rating plus tranche thickness, effective for RBC reporting as of 31 December 2026, with an 11.77% pretax surcharge on below-investment-grade BSL CLO tranches of 4% thickness or less, thickness measured on a current basis from the most recent trustee report, no floor at current bond C-1 factors, and the 45% residual charge retained.
frame_summary: Sidley is arguing that the NAIC has moved insurer capital for structured and collateral-backed assets onto asset-specific, structure-sensitive mechanics, so that the capital outcome now depends on features of the instrument that the credit rating does not by itself convey.
verbatim_quote: measured on a current basis, using the most recent trustee report
verbatim_list: Tranche thickness is measured on a current basis, using the most recent trustee report available as of the investment reporting date rather than as of origination.
An 11.77% pretax surcharge will apply to below-investment-grade tranches (NAIC Designation Category 2.C or below) of only BSL CLOs (not middle market CLOs) with a thickness of 4% or less.
The existing 45% pretax charge for CLO residual tranches is retained.

adopted revisions to the RBC charges for collateral loans that replace the existing uniform 6.8% RBC charge on all collateral loans with a framework that bases the applicable RBC charge on the collateral underlying such collateral loan, effective for RBC reported as of year-end December 31, 2027

title: NAIC moves to adopt new RBC factors for CLO investments
date_evidence: meta-insight_date: 2026-06-30T00:00:00Z; on-page dateline "30 June 2026 - 5 minute read"
key_claim: The 23 June 2026 vote closed a project running since early 2022. Senior investment-grade tranches generally see reduced charges relative to the current corporate-bond regime, particularly AAA through A, while lower-rated tranches face materially higher charges plus the thin-tranche surcharge. DLA Piper reads the vote as moving CLO capital treatment away from a purely ratings-based framework toward modelled risk and structural features, so that identical ratings need not produce identical RBC outcomes, and expects the framework to become a reference point for future NAIC work on rated feeders and related asset-backed structures.
frame_summary: DLA Piper is arguing that the significance of the June vote is directional rather than numerical: the NAIC has established that a credit rating is an input to the capital charge rather than the determinant of it, and market participants should expect that principle to travel to other structured asset classes.
verbatim_quote: similar ratings would not necessarily produce similar RBC outcomes
verbatim_list: The NAIC vote moves CLO capital treatment away from a purely ratings-based framework and toward a capital regime that gives greater weight to modeled risk and structural features.
Under the new framework, similar ratings would not necessarily produce similar RBC outcomes.
For senior investment-grade tranches, the adopted factors generally reduce RBC charges relative to the current regime for corporate bonds, particularly for AAA through A-rated securities.
marking the principal decision point in a project that began in early 2022
Notably, the new CLO RBC framework may also become a reference point for future NAIC work on other structured products, including rated feeders and related asset-backed securities structures.

title: Financial regulators need to get ahead of the curve on private credit
date_evidence: On-page byline block: "Expert comment / Published 15 July 2026 - 3 minute READ"; image path /2026-07/2026-07-15-private-credit-169117081.jpg
key_claim: Private credit is between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion on a narrow definition and possibly $10 trillion to $50 trillion on a broad one, having grown from around $40 billion in 2000. Concentration is high: five large asset managers account for a third of aggregate loan commitments globally. Insurance is a principal transmission channel, with private-equity-based insurers controlling nearly $900 billion of US liabilities against $67 billion in 2012. Khatri argues the asset class is lightly regulated, untested by a full credit cycle, and that opaque layered leverage may make systemic risk larger than headline size suggests.
frame_summary: Chatham House is arguing that private credit is on a path to systemic importance through its links to banks, insurers and retail savings, and that the binding regulatory deficiency is data and definitional: supervisors cannot yet measure the exposure they would need to contain.
verbatim_quote: Globally, five large asset managers account for one-third of aggregate loan commitments in the private credit sector.
verbatim_list: private equity-based insurers control nearly $900 billion in liabilities
Private credit is lightly regulated and untested by a genuine credit cycle, let alone a deep and prolonged economic downturn.

title: Private Credit and Life-Insurer Solvency: Evidence for a Calibrated Regulatory Approach
date_evidence: Author byline block: "Lawrence Powell & Julian Morris June 5, 2026"; meta-article:modified_time: 2026-06-09T13:29:15+00:00
key_claim: Powell and Morris present regression evidence that life insurers with larger private-debt allocations exhibit stronger, not weaker, financial profiles, and argue the available evidence does not support the view that private credit creates risks existing insurance regulation fails to capture. They criticise the NAIC's revised CLO RBC treatment as using model assumptions substantially more conservative than those in the corporate-bond framework, note the project was not motivated by poor historical performance, and warn that classifying segments with insufficient data as high risk penalises private markets for being private. They call for prospective, narrowly targeted remedies with grandfathering and transition periods longer than three to six months.
frame_summary: ICLE is arguing that the empirical case for tightening insurer capital treatment of private credit has not been made, and that regulators should calibrate to observed risk rather than to the opacity of the asset class, because a data gap is a supervisory problem and not evidence of credit risk.
verbatim_quote: The NAIC recently revised RBC treatment for collateralized loan obligations (CLOs) using model assumptions that appear substantially more conservative than those embedded in the framework used for corporate bonds.
verbatim_list: Notably, this project was not motivated by poor historical performance.
The available evidence therefore does not support the view that private credit creates risks existing insurance regulation fails to capture.
That approach risks systematically penalizing private markets because they are private.

title: Insurers are funding AI infrastructure, and the NAIC wants to know if the ratings hold up
key_claim: The NAIC is reviewing insurers' data-centre holdings and the credit ratings underpinning them, examining tenant creditworthiness, lease exit clauses and construction records. Since January 2026 it has held the power to challenge and override ratings that differ from its own analysis by more than three notches, covering public and private ratings. Bonds with private placement numbers made up 23.4% of insurers' total admitted bonds in 2025 against 18.3% in 2021 on S&P Global Market Intelligence data, and about 20% of US life insurers' fixed-income portfolios are linked to private and illiquid bonds on Moody's data. The Valuation of Securities Task Force was reorganised into four groups at the start of 2026 and Treasury Secretary Bessent met state commissioners in May 2026.
frame_summary: Insurance Business is arguing that the data-centre review exposes a reflexive tension: the NAIC helped create the regulatory conditions that made privately rated infrastructure debt attractive to insurers, and now holds the power to withdraw the rating on which that attractiveness rests.
verbatim_quote: Since January, the NAIC has held the power to challenge and override credit ratings where they differ from its own analysis by more than three rating notches, covering both public and private ratings.
verbatim_list: Bonds with private placement numbers made up 23.4% of insurers' total admitted bonds in 2025, up from 18.3% in 2021, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence.
About 20% of US life insurers' fixed-income portfolios are linked to private and illiquid bonds, according to Moody's Ratings cited by the FT

The rating, in other words, is not just a label. It determines how much capital an insurer must hold against the position, and therefore how attractive the investment appears on a risk-adjusted basis.

title: Warren presses insurance regulators for answers on private credit ties as Walter probe widens
key_claim: Senator Elizabeth Warren wrote to NAIC chief executive Jeffrey Johnston on 11 September 2026 asking how the association will police ties between private investment firms and the life insurers they own. Delaware Life had reported related-party holdings of roughly 3% of investments, about $1.4 billion, and after an internal review prompted by grand jury subpoenas corrected the figure to more than $17 billion, upwards of 39% of total invested assets. Warren cited NAIC data showing life insurers' private credit holdings rising from $386 billion in 2014 to $849 billion in 2024, and said the NAIC had initiated only modest reforms, many still under development.
frame_summary: Insurance Business is arguing that federal political attention has now attached to the reliability of what insurers themselves report about affiliated and private assets, which raises the probability that disclosure and designation standards tighten rather than loosen from here.
verbatim_quote: In her letter, Warren cited NAIC data showing that life insurers' private credit holdings climbed from $386 billion in 2014 to $849 billion in 2024, more than doubling over the decade.
